summary: Describes UTF-8, a way to encode Unicode and ISO 10646 characters as bytes that preserves the full US-ASCII range. This version is informational and was replaced by RFC 2279.

eli5.summary: UTF-8 writes letters from every language using plain bytes, and plain English letters stay just as they were.

subtitle: A byte-oriented encoding that represents Unicode characters while preserving ASCII compatibility.

tldr.problem: Unicode and ISO 10646 define a 16-bit character set for the world's writing systems, but 16-bit characters are incompatible with many applications and protocols that assume 8-bit bytes. Existing 7-bit mail systems also cannot handle arbitrary binary data.
tldr.mechanism: UTF-8 encodes Unicode characters using 1 to 6 bytes, with ASCII characters (0x00 to 0x7F) always encoded as a single byte matching their ASCII value. Multi-byte sequences use a prefix to indicate the total length, allowing the decoder to recognize character boundaries and detect errors.
tldr.outcome: UTF-8 became the standard encoding for Unicode on the web and in most internet protocols, providing transparent compatibility with ASCII while supporting all 1.1 million characters in Unicode and ISO 10646.

today: RFC 2044 was replaced by RFC 2279, which provided an updated specification. UTF-8 became the de facto standard encoding for internationalized text on the internet and is now used in HTML, email, JSON, and virtually all internet protocols.

sections.title: The Challenge of Unicode
sections.content:
Unicode and ISO 10646 define character sets with 65,536 characters (16-bit UCS-2) and up to 2 billion characters (31-bit UCS-4), encompassing writing systems from around the world. However, these wide character sets create a problem: most applications, protocols, file systems, and network code assume 8-bit bytes or even 7-bit ASCII. Sending 16-bit characters through email, over networks, or into parsers built for 7-bit text breaks compatibility.

Several UCS transformation formats (UTF) were proposed to solve this. UTF-1 became obsolete. UTF-7 encodes the full Unicode repertoire using only 7-bit ASCII-safe bytes but is inefficient. UTF-16 uses 16-bit units for some characters and surrogate pairs for others. UTF-8, the subject of this memo, uses variable-length byte sequences while preserving full ASCII compatibility.
sections.eli5: The world has many languages with many more characters than English. Unicode tried to fit them all into 16-bit numbers, but that doesn't work with the networks and programs we have, which work best with simple bytes. UTF-8 found a clever trick: use variable-length byte sequences that keep English the same.

sections.title: How UTF-8 Encoding Works
sections.content:
UTF-8 encodes characters using 1 to 6 bytes. For ASCII characters (0x00 to 0x7F), a single byte is used with the high bit set to 0. For multi-byte sequences, the first byte has leading 1 bits indicating the sequence length, followed by a 0 bit (for example, 110xxxxx for a 2-byte sequence). Continuation bytes in the sequence always start with 10xxxxxx, leaving 6 bits for the character value in each continuation byte.

For example, ASCII 'A' (0x41) encodes as the single byte 0x41. The Euro sign (U+20AC) encodes as three bytes: 0xE2 0x82 0xAC. The pattern allows a decoder to determine the sequence length from the first byte alone, find character boundaries by scanning for start bytes (without 10 prefix), and detect truncation or invalid sequences.

Round-trip conversion between UTF-8 and UCS-2 or UCS-4 is straightforward. The only special case is that UCS-2 values in the range 0xD800-0xDFFF, which are UTF-16 surrogate pairs in ISO 10646, require special handling: the surrogate pair must be converted to a UCS-4 character before encoding to UTF-8.
sections.eli5: UTF-8 uses variable-length byte groups. English stays one byte. Other letters from other languages become 2, 3, or more bytes. The first byte of a group tells you how long the group is, so programs can always tell where one character starts and the next begins.

sections.title: Key Properties and Advantages
sections.content:
UTF-8 has several critical properties that made it ideal for internet protocols. US-ASCII values (0x00 to 0x7F) never appear in multi-byte sequences, only as single-byte ASCII characters. This means any octet with the high bit clear (bytes 0x00 to 0x7F) is always ASCII, providing transparency to ASCII-based systems like file systems, parsers (printf in C), and network protocols.

Character boundaries are easy to find by scanning for start bytes (those not starting with 10). UTF-8 preserves the lexicographic sort order of UCS-4 strings, meaning strings with multi-byte characters sort the same way as their UCS-4 representation. The octet values 0xFE and 0xFF never appear in UTF-8, which is useful for distinguishing UTF-8 from UTF-16 encodings.

These properties combine to make UTF-8 the encoding of choice for environments that historically relied on 8-bit bytes: Unix systems, file systems, email, and the web. Unlike UTF-16, UTF-8 requires no byte-order mark and poses no problems with endianness. Unlike UTF-7, it is efficient for ASCII-heavy content.
sections.eli5: UTF-8 is clever: English text looks exactly the same. Programs that don't know about UTF-8 still work fine with English. And you can always find where one character ends and the next starts just by looking at the bytes.

sections.title: Encoding Examples
sections.content:
The RFC provides concrete examples of UTF-8 encoding. The ASCII letter 'A' (U+0041) encodes as a single byte: 0x41. The space and period also encode as single bytes: 0x20 and 0x2E.

The character 'α' (U+03B1, Greek small letter alpha) encodes as two bytes: 0xCE 0xB1. The Unicode character 'β' (U+03B2) encodes as 0xCE 0xB2.

Multi-byte examples include the Euro sign '€' (U+20AC), which encodes as 0xE2 0x82 0xAC. The Japanese Hiragana 'A' (U+3042 Hiragana Letter A) encodes as 0xE3 0x81 0x82. These examples illustrate how the byte sequence length increases for characters with larger code points, yet all ASCII characters remain single bytes.
sections.eli5: An English letter like 'A' is one byte: 0x41. A Greek letter is two bytes. A Japanese character is three bytes. You can tell how many bytes a letter needs just by looking at the first byte.

sections.title: MIME Charset Registration
sections.content:
This memo serves as the basis for registering UTF-8 as a MIME charset parameter. The proposed name is 'UTF-8', allowing email, web pages, and other MIME content to declare that their text is encoded in UTF-8. This registration enables mail clients, web browsers, and other applications to correctly handle internationalized content while preserving backward compatibility with ASCII.

The UTF-8 charset registration allows Internet protocols and applications to standardize on a single encoding for Unicode, eliminating confusion between UTF-7, UTF-16, and other variants. By October 1996, UTF-8 was ready to become the standard way to send international text over the internet.
sections.eli5: UTF-8 got a name so programs could recognize it. Email and web pages can now say 'this text is UTF-8' and programs know how to read it correctly.
